notes:
Docket said a rule of yours had stopped working, when the rule underneath it was doing the job.

Some sites write robots.txt rules aimed at AI crawlers that have since changed their name. Anthropic's crawler is no longer `anthropic-ai`, Webz.io's is no longer `omgili`. A rule addressed to the old name is read by nobody: the file is valid, no tool warns, and the line sits there looking like a decision you made. Docket finds those, and that part has not changed.

What changed is what it says they cost you.

If a `User-agent` line naming a dead crawler sat above a `Disallow`, Docket called it a medium-severity problem and told you those crawlers were reading pages you meant to withhold. It reached that conclusion without looking at the rest of your file — specifically without reading your `User-agent: *` group, which is where a crawler goes when no rule names it.

On a computer manufacturer's site we audited, the difference mattered. Six dead names, all genuinely dead. Their group carried seven `Disallow` rules — and every one of those seven was also in the site's `*` group, which carries seventeen. So those crawlers were falling back to *stricter* rules than the ones addressed to their old names, and nothing was being read that anyone meant to withhold. The site's own `ClaudeBot` line sat in the same group as the retired `Claude-Web`, covering the same crawler under the name it actually sends.

The finding was true. The consequence was not, and the severity rested on the consequence.

Docket now reads the fallback before deciding. A dead name over rules your `*` group already carries, or sitting beside the crawler's current name, is reported as what it is: an inert line that reads like a policy you have not actually set — worth tidying, not worth alarm. **A dead name over a rule that genuinely would stop being enforced is still reported at the old severity**, because that one really does leave a door open.

If your robots.txt has no `*` group at all, nothing changes either: there is no fallback, so every rule under a dead name really is lost, and Docket says so.

**Also:** an internal check that confirms the app you installed is the one we shipped now also confirms it was signed by us. Verifying a signature is intact is not the same as verifying whose it is, and only the first was automatic.
